newsitem.title: UK: Schroders in pioneering rights issue tender.
newsitem.headline: Schroders in pioneering rights issue tender.

text.p: After a succesful test run last week, merchant bank Schroders Plc on Tuesday launched a second rights issue for a British company with a feature that allows variable underwriting fees and offers new flexibility.

Built into a plan intended to raise 48.6 million pounds ($80.3 million) for advertising company More Group Plc, Schroders invited tenders for competitive bids, based on fees, from institutions interested in underwriting the share offer.

This innovative tender mechanism leaves the conventional relationships between client, banks and institutions intact but adds a new dimension to deals and addresses some of the concerns of British regulators who feel existing practices are too rigid.
Until last week the only means for companies seeking to raise funds to set the balance of risk and reward for investors has been through the price level at which it offers its shares.

With a tender, proponents say, companies are able to try varying the fees with which they reward those prepared to protect their whole transaction from the risk of failure -- specifically the sub-underwriters.

Under conventional practice, primary underwriters like Schroders offer out the sub-underwriting of a transaction to institutional investors, normally those who may have an interest in holding some of the stock should the main offer fail.
They in turn demand fixed fees for this and, usually, these have been rolled into an overall cost of about 2.0 percent of the transaction value for all the arrangers and underwriters.
According to market sources the sub-underwriters' part has, in fact, made up over half of this total, while fee tendering can bring this portion of the cost under one percent.

While not confirming the impact on fee levels, a Schroders spokesman told Reuters: "Schroders has sought to preserve the best elements of the sub-underwriting system, and the tender process is designed to minimise the risk of a large proportion of a company's shares being left in loose hands."
Last Thursday the bank broke new ground in UK institutional underwriting when it used a tender within a 222 million pound rights issue for hotels group Stakis Plc.
The main result was to reduce the commission bill for Stakis, as the bank passed on pro-rata the reductions it achieved in the total sub-underwriting commissions.
It said the saving amounted to about 400,000 pounds, leaving the company with an underwriting fee bill of 4.2 million pounds.
There are two underlying concerns which the trials of this type of system hope they can address, bankers say.

On the one hand, lead banks will have to be careful not to be too free with their tendering and prioritise lower fees over suitable investors as this could seriously undermine a company's share price in the event of the main transaction failing.
Banking groups therefore expect that, as Schroders has done, they will closely manage the tender process and put upward limits on the allotment of shares sub-underwriters can seek.

"We believe that the careful choice of sub-underwriting institutions and the use of prudent limits on the exposure of individual sub-underwriters have always been important parts of the underwriting process," the Schroders spokesman added.
On the other hand, the innovation comes at a time when the entire underwriting system is under scrutiny and under an implicit threat from regulators to change or be changed.

The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) has been considering referring the system for study by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission, but has said it is waiting to see how institutions react to initiatives that result in greater flexibility.
